1.pericope_label: Then Jesus six days before the passover came to Bethany, where Lazarus was which had been dead, whom he raised from the dead. There they made him a supper; and Martha served: but Lazarus was one of them that sat at the table with him. Then took Mary a pound of ointment of spikenard, very costly, and anointed the feet of Jesus, and wiped his feet with her hair: and the house was filled with the odour of the ointment. Then saith one of his disciples, Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, which should betray him, Why was not this ointment sold for three hundred pence, and given to the poor? This he said, not that he cared for the poor; but because he was a thief, and had the bag, and bare what was put therein. Then said Jesus, Let her alone: against the day of my burying hath she kept this. For the poor always ye have with you; but me ye have not always.

schools.summary: Robertson dates the supper from the crucifixion, so that six days before falls on the preceding sabbath or the Friday afternoon, identifies the pound as the Roman litra against the alabaster cruse of the other accounts, takes the disputed adjective for genuine, and sets out the harder problem that Mark and Matthew place this supper two days before the passover where John puts it on the arrival at Bethany, reporting Bernard's judgment that John is more probably accurate. Barnes follows the earlier Gospels in putting it at the house of Simon the leper, notes that Martha and Lazarus are named because it was not their own house and that Lazarus at table proves his restoration no illusion, and explains the bag from the case in which musicians kept their pipe-reeds. Ellicott observes that John alone leaves the place undefined while adding that Martha served and Lazarus was present, and that Matthew ascribes the objection to the disciples and Mark to certain persons where John remembers it was Judas. Lightfoot builds the week out from the sabbath's going out, when suppers were more liberal, and traces the word for the bag through the Talmudists to a coffer for money.

Calvin holds that the ointment was no simple extract but a compound of many odoriferous substances, and reports from Pliny that ordinary ointment cost ten denarii where the best reached three hundred and ten, so Judas valued it correctly; he thinks the murmuring came from Judas alone and the others were induced to assent, since slander is readily embraced, and insists on the distinction between Mary's extraordinary action and the daily service due to Christ, calling those apes rather than imitators who serve him by costly display. Gill reckons the three hundred pence in English money.

Clarke presses the verb for carrying the bag further than the others, arguing from its use elsewhere that Judas did not merely carry what was put in but stole it, and joins Ellicott and Robertson in preferring the reading that she may keep the ointment for the day of the embalming. Wesley makes the sixth day before the passover the sabbath the Jews called the Great Sabbath.
Henry takes the visit as a preface to the passover, devout men setting time apart beforehand to prepare for a solemnity.

Chrysostom looks past the price of the ointment to the manner of the giver, since Mary did not take part in the general serving but gave all her attention to the Lord, treating him not as mere man but as God; on the last verse he broadens the warning from wealth to power, the one breeding covetousness and the other pride, and notes that here the multitude believes where the rulers do not.

Augustine takes the last clause of bodily presence only, since in majesty and invisible grace the promise holds that he is with us to the end of the world, and finds in Judas a figure of the wicked within the Church.

debates.question: Is this the supper the earlier Gospels place two days before the passover?

positions.position: Yes, and John's dating is the more probably accurate
Yes, and it was at the house of Simon the leper, not of Lazarus

debates.question: What does Jesus tell them to let her do?

positions.position: Keep the ointment for the day of the embalming, on the better manuscripts
Nothing further: she has already kept it against that day

outliers.claim: Argues from the verb's use elsewhere that Judas did not merely carry the bag but stole from it, going beyond the other witnesses

There they made him a supper; and Martha served: but Lazarus was one of them that sat at the table with him.
Then took Mary a pound of ointment of spikenard, very costly, and anointed the feet of Jesus, and wiped his feet with her hair: and the house was filled with the odour of the ointment.

Why was not this ointment sold for three hundred pence, and given to the poor?
This he said, not that he cared for the poor; but because he was a thief, and had the bag, and bare what was put therein.

9.pericope_label: Much people of the Jews therefore knew that he was there: and they came not for Jesus’ sake only, but that they might see Lazarus also, whom he had raised from the dead. But the chief priests consulted that they might put Lazarus also to death; Because that by reason of him many of the Jews went away, and believed on Jesus.

schools.summary: Ellicott supposes pilgrims from Jericho carried the news to people already asking after him, notes that many came to see Lazarus as well, observes that the chief priests were mostly Sadducees so that the living Lazarus contradicted their own doctrine of no resurrection, and reads the closing tenses as a continuing secession, two words marking a withdrawal from the priests' authority and a faith in Jesus. Barnes states the principle that when men are determined not to believe there is no end to the crimes they are driven to, the witness having to be removed although no charge could be brought against him. Robertson stops at the odd placing of the article in the phrase for the crowd, reporting Westcott's suggestion that the words had become a compound noun, calls the last verb an inchoative imperfect, and guesses that the Sadducees reasoned that if they killed both, Lazarus at least would stay dead.

Gill points out that Bethany lay only two miles from Jerusalem so the report soon reached the city, and keeps in view that the man himself was the living and abiding witness of the miracle. Calvin reads the whole celebrity as providential, since the nearer the death approached the more necessary it was that the name of Christ should be widely known, and God intended so remarkable a proof of his divinity to have many witnesses.

Clarke notes the habit of this Gospel of giving the name of Jews to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and puts the plot as an absurdity, that they were blind not to see that he who had raised the man after four days could raise him again though they killed him a thousand times. Wesley draws the inference nobody else makes, that here is the plain reason why the earlier evangelists, writing while Lazarus was still alive, did not tell his story.

debates.question: Why kill Lazarus, against whom nothing could be charged?

positions.position: Because the evidence was irresistible and the witness had to be removed before the death of Jesus could be managed quietly
Because ungodliness, once prevailing, becomes a spirit of giddiness with which Satan torments the wicked
Because the Sadducees may have reasoned that killing both would keep Lazarus dead

outliers.claim: Explains the silence of the earlier Gospels about Lazarus by the danger he stood in while they were written

themes: Much people of the Jews therefore knew that he was there: and they came not for Jesus’ sake only, but that they might see Lazarus also, whom he had raised from the dead.
But the chief priests consulted that they might put Lazarus also to death;
Because that by reason of him many of the Jews went away, and believed on Jesus.

12.pericope_label: On the next day much people that were come to the feast, when they heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem, Took branches of palm trees, and went forth to meet him, and cried, Hosanna: Blessed is the King of Israel that cometh in the name of the Lord. And Jesus, when he had found a young ass, sat thereon; as it is written, Fear not, daughter of Sion: behold, thy King cometh, sitting on an ass’s colt. These things understood not his disciples at the first: but when Jesus was glorified, then remembered they that these things were written of him, and that they had done these things unto him. The people therefore that was with him when he called Lazarus out of his grave, and raised him from the dead, bare record. For this cause the people also met him, for that they heard that he had done this miracle. The Pharisees therefore said among themselves, Perceive ye how ye prevail nothing? behold, the world is gone after him.

schools.summary: Robertson dates the day to Palm Sunday and takes the phrase for the common people rather than a great multitude, agrees that rightly understood Matthew has Jesus riding the colt only, and adds the force of the prophecy, that the ass was ridden in peace as the horse in war. Ellicott observes that John alone gives this note of time, tying the entry to the stay at Bethany, renders the palms literally as the palm branches of the palm trees and notes that neither word occurs elsewhere in the New Testament, calls the disciples' later understanding a touch exactly in John's manner, and distinguishes the crowd that had been at the grave from the multitude that came out on hearing of it. Barnes glosses the glorifying as the resurrection and ascension, and takes the Pharisees' word about the world as an idiom for the bulk of the people. Lightfoot supplies a rabbinic estimate of the passover throng, King Agrippa counting the lambs by having one kidney of each laid aside and reaching six hundred thousand pair, and notes that the Talmudists speak in the same way of all the world going after a man.

Calvin treats the branches as an emblem of victory and peace and the shout as a confession, since the psalm quoted was composed with reference to the Messiah; he resolves the apparent contradiction between the Gospels about the animals by taking Matthew's account as a synecdoche, gives the figure of the seed that does not spring as soon as it is sown for the disciples' slowness, and hears in the Pharisees' despair men reproaching their own slothfulness to work themselves up to extremity, drawing the lesson that if the enemies of God persevere so obstinately in evil we ought to be far steadier in a just undertaking. Gill calls it a crowded passover, every male being obliged to appear and multitudes of women coming besides.

Clarke takes the Pharisees' word about the world as the common idiom for everybody, comparing the French phrase, and makes the general rule that only in the light of the new covenant is the old fully understood. Wesley says the crowd were chiefly Galileans and not men of Jerusalem, finds in the meekness of the prophecy a reason that forbids fear, and draws the practical rule that the design of God's dispensations is seldom understood at first, so the great work of faith is to embrace what we shall know hereafter.
Henry makes the point with an edge, that these were country people from remote parts, the nearer the temple the further from the Lord of the temple.
Chrysostom draws the calendar out of the law: the lamb was shut up on the tenth day and killed on the fourteenth, and so the spotless Lamb went up to Jerusalem five days before his immolation.

debates.question: Who made up the crowd that met him?

positions.position: Country people and Galileans come up for the feast, not inhabitants of Jerusalem
Two distinct crowds, one following from the grave of Lazarus and one going out to meet him

outliers.claim: Fixes the day by the paschal lamb's four days of keeping, so that the entry falls five days before the immolation

Took branches of palm trees, and went forth to meet him, and cried, Hosanna: Blessed is the King of Israel that cometh in the name of the Lord.
And Jesus, when he had found a young ass, sat thereon; as it is written,

20.pericope_label: And there were certain Greeks among them that came up to worship at the feast: The same came therefore to Philip, which was of Bethsaida of Galilee, and desired him, saying, Sir, we would see Jesus. Philip cometh and telleth Andrew: and again Andrew and Philip tell Jesus. And Jesus answered them, saying, The hour is come, that the Son of man should be glorified. Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit. He that loveth his life shall lose it; and he that hateth his life in this world shall keep it unto life eternal. If any man serve me, let him follow me; and where I am, there shall also my servant be: if any man serve me, him will my Father honour.

schools.summary: Ellicott and Robertson insist the word means Hellenes and not Hellenists, taking the enquirers for God-fearers admitted to Judaism's privileges; Ellicott finds it striking that they came to the only two apostles bearing Greek names, calls the reply the utterance of his own thoughts rather than an answer though he thinks the Greeks heard it, treats the grain of wheat as an instance of one law of life given to the moral and physical worlds alike, and prefers the present tense in the hard saying, so that the man who loves his life is losing it already. Robertson calls Andrew a man of wisdom for a crisis, names the middle wall of partition that would later puzzle Peter at Joppa, identifies the hour as the predestined one, and denies any borrowing from the Eleusinian mysteries, noting that Paul uses the same figure of the resurrection. Barnes sets out the three opinions about who the Greeks were, and takes the verse about following into persecution. Lightfoot narrows the guess to Syro-Grecians of Decapolis or Gadara, and paraphrases the logic that makes the grain of wheat an answer at all.

Calvin dissents from the Gentile reading on legal grounds, since Roman law punished a man who left his native worship for the Jewish; he reads the indirect approach through Philip as reverence, which always begets modesty, takes the glorifying not of the death but of the publication of the gospel, presses the paradox that sowing appears to destroy the seed and is the cause of far more abundant increase, and defines the terms of the hard saying, that the man who cannot leave the world except by constraint loves his life. Gill keeps it plain, that a man so in love with this life as to deny the faith loses both.

Clarke sets out the same three opinions about the Greeks and expects the disciple who lays down his life to receive it with everlasting honour. Wesley cares only what they signify, a prelude of the Gentile Church, observes that out of thousands of seeds our Lord singles out almost the only one which dies in the earth, matched only by millet and the large bean, and adds the one qualification to the hour of glory, that he must suffer first.
Henry dates the visit a day or two after the entry, that day having been taken up with public work.
Chrysostom says the present life is sweet only to those riveted to it, since a man who looks at the beauty of heaven despises it as a lesser beauty when a greater appears.
Bede supplies the setting, the temple being famous enough to draw Gentiles from distant countries, the eunuch of Candace among them.

debates.question: Were the Greeks who asked for Jesus Gentiles?

positions.position: Yes, Hellenes and not Hellenists, proselytes of the gate admitted to worship
Probably not uncircumcised, since Roman law punished conversion to the Jewish religion
The question is open: three opinions can be maintained

debates.question: What is the hour that is come?

positions.position: The predestined hour of the death, seen from the beginning as not yet come
Rather the publication of the gospel through the world, so the disciples should not lose courage

outliers.claim: Observes as a naturalist that of all the thousands of seeds our Lord chose almost the only one which dies in the earth, matched only by millet and the large bean

themes: And there were certain Greeks among them that came up to worship at the feast:
The same came therefore to Philip, which was of Bethsaida of Galilee, and desired him, saying, Sir, we would see Jesus.
Philip cometh and telleth Andrew: and again Andrew and Philip tell Jesus.
And Jesus answered them, saying, The hour is come, that the Son of man should be glorified.
Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.
He that loveth his life shall lose it; and he that hateth his life in this world shall keep it unto life eternal.
If any man serve me, let him follow me; and where I am, there shall also my servant be: if any man serve me, him will my Father honour.

27.pericope_label: Now is my soul troubled; and what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour: but for this cause came I unto this hour. Father, glorify thy name. Then came there a voice from heaven, saying, I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again. The people therefore, that stood by, and heard it, said that it thundered: others said, An angel spake to him. Jesus answered and said, This voice came not because of me, but for your sakes. Now is the judgment of this world: now shall the prince of this world be cast out. And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me. This he said, signifying what death he should die.

schools.summary: Robertson observes that John, proving the deity throughout, everywhere assumes the humanity, and gives no Gethsemane because this stands in its place; he calls the prayer that follows the prayer of the spirit against the flesh, notes that there is no article with the judgement so that it is a judgement and not the judgement, and adds that Satan had claimed the world in the temptation and is here proclaimed defeated. Ellicott makes the pronoun of the prayer emphatic and compares the Lord's Prayer, argues from the preservation of what the crowd thought that the narrative was written by one present, since a later hand would have had no motive for it, and makes the pronoun of the last saying strongly emphatic, the conqueror set against the vanquished. Barnes hears intense anxiety in the broken question, and explains the two reports of the voice, some taking it for a natural phenomenon and others recalling the Jewish opinion that God speaks only through angels. Lightfoot shows that the phrase for the prince of this world was common among the Jewish writers, who meant the angel into whose hands the world was delivered.

Calvin admits the troubled soul seems to contradict the courage just urged on the disciples and answers that it is in perfect harmony, as every believer knows by experience; he calls it monstrous that so evident a miracle left the assembly unmoved and says the same happens daily, hears in the word for judgement not condemnation but the restoring of a well-ordered state, and turns the lifting up into an image, the cross being a chariot by which he raises men with himself to the Father. Gill hears the brazen serpent in the lifting up and reads a violent, public death.

Clarke says he took our weaknesses that he might sanctify them and that nature abhors death by God's own implanting, takes the name for God himself in all his attributes, reports Bishop Pearce's guess that there was thunder as well as a voice and Wetstein's that the voice came in a language unintelligible to Greeks, and refers the judgement to the punishment about to fall on the Jewish nation. Wesley denies that the broken question means what shall I choose, since the heart was fixed on the Father's will and he laboured rather for utterance, parses the answer from heaven into halves, and draws from the divided crowd the lesson that in the most glorious revelations something may remain obscure to exercise faith.
Henry marks the strangeness of the word, coming in the middle of pleasing prospects where one would expect him to say his soul was pleased.

Chrysostom supplies the objection the troubled soul answers, that the disciples might have said it was easy for one beyond the reach of pain to talk philosophically about death; so he lets them see that he is himself in an agony and yet will not decline it merely to relieve himself.

debates.question: What does the word rendered judgement mean here?

positions.position: A judgement rather than the judgement, the coming days being the test of this world
The punishment about to fall on the Jewish nation
Not condemnation at all but the restoring of a well-ordered state, on the Hebrew sense of the term

debates.question: Why did some hear only thunder?

positions.position: Because there was thunder as well as a voice, and those at a distance heard only the one
Because they were dull of hearing, as many are still unmoved by the Gospel
Because something may remain obscure in the clearest revelation, to exercise faith

outliers.claim: Turns the crowd's confusion into an argument for authorship, since the preservation of what bystanders thought at the time runs against everything a later writer would want

themes: Now is my soul troubled; and what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour: but for this cause came I unto this hour.
Father, glorify thy name. Then came there a voice from heaven, saying, I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again.
The people therefore, that stood by, and heard it, said that it thundered: others said, An angel spake to him.
Jesus answered and said, This voice came not because of me, but for your sakes.
Now is the judgment of this world: now shall the prince of this world be cast out.
And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me.
This he said, signifying what death he should die.

34.pericope_label: The people answered him, We have heard out of the law that Christ abideth for ever: and how sayest thou, The Son of man must be lifted up? who is this Son of man? Then Jesus said unto them, Yet a little while is the light with you. Walk while ye have the light, lest darkness come upon you: for he that walketh in darkness knoweth not whither he goeth. While ye have light, believe in the light, that ye may be the children of light. These things spake Jesus, and departed, and did hide himself from them.

schools.summary: Ellicott agrees the term law covers the whole Old Testament and finds in the objection a specimen of rabbinic theology, reading the promises of an abiding kingdom as a temporal reign; he prefers to render the connecting word therefore rather than then, observes that the narrative does not say he answered them, and would render the closing exhortation according as ye have the light, taking becoming sons of light for the familiar thought that the believer grows like the one he believes in. Barnes traces the objection to the interpreters and points to the passages promising a priest for ever and an everlasting dominion, and reads the indirection as tact, since Jesus never roused men's prejudices needlessly nor shrank from unpalatable truth. Robertson says plainly that he would not argue theology with a crowd who could not follow it, and identifies sons of light as a Hebrew idiom amounting to enlightened men. Lightfoot explains the appeal as a formula, out of the law being set against out of the scribes, and turns their text against the rabbis, who fixed the length of Messiah's days at forty years, or seventy, or three generations.

Calvin grants both halves of the prophecy and blames the selection, since it was plainly said that Christ would die and that his kingdom would afterwards flourish, but they seize the second clause alone and malice blinds them in the clearest light; he hears both admonition and sharp reproof in the reply, insists that the light meant is not the bodily presence but the Gospel, and explains that the withdrawal at the end was from the adversaries, not from the disciples. Gill calls the questioners cavillers.

Clarke denies the premise outright, that no part of Scripture ever said the Messiah should not die while several say expressly that he must, keeps the figure of the light moving as one about to disappear for a short time and afterwards to shine with greater lustre, presses the sonship hard, that as truly as a child partakes of his parent's nature so they were to have nothing in them but truth and righteousness, and will not have a miracle in the hiding where a withdrawal suffices. Wesley reconciles the two halves in a line, that he first dies and then abides for ever, and makes the light I and my doctrine.
Henry puts the failure more gently, that they drew false notions from Scripture by overlooking the prophecies of his suffering.
Chrysostom treats the question as bad faith rather than error, since deceit is weak and easily detected however it be daubed with ten thousand colours, like whitewash on a decayed wall.

Augustine notes that the crowd understood him to be speaking of his own death, and that though he had not used the title in the sentence they challenge, they remembered how often he used it of himself.

debates.question: How is the objection from the law to be met?

positions.position: By denying its premise: Scripture nowhere says the Messiah would not die, and says expressly that he must
By holding both halves together: he first dies and then abides for ever
By treating the question as bad faith rather than a difficulty at all

outliers.claim: Grants the questioners their text and turns it against the rabbis, who had fixed the Messiah's days at forty years, seventy, or three generations

themes: The people answered him, We have heard out of the law that Christ abideth for ever: and how sayest thou, The Son of man must be lifted up? who is this Son of man?
Then Jesus said unto them, Yet a little while is the light with you. Walk while ye have the light, lest darkness come upon you: for he that walketh in darkness knoweth not whither he goeth.
While ye have light, believe in the light, that ye may be the children of light. These things spake Jesus, and departed, and did hide himself from them.

37.pericope_label: But though he had done so many miracles before them, yet they believed not on him: That the saying of Esaias the prophet might be fulfilled, which he spake, Lord, who hath believed our report? and to whom hath the arm of the Lord been revealed? Therefore they could not believe, because that Esaias said again, He hath blinded their eyes, and hardened their heart; that they should not see with their eyes, nor understand with their heart, and be converted, and I should heal them. These things said Esaias, when he saw his glory, and spake of him. Nevertheless among the chief rulers also many believed on him; but because of the Pharisees they did not confess him, lest they should be put out of the synagogue: For they loved the praise of men more than the praise of God.

schools.summary: Barnes reads the verse not of miracles wrought that day but of all the works done in the nation's sight, John giving the result of the ministry; he takes the word could as the Bible often uses it, of an obstacle that makes a result certain, reads the prophet's commission as a message whose effect, given the hardness of the hearers, would be to blind them, and agrees they did not reject him so that a prophecy might be fulfilled but that by rejecting him the same thing happened as in Isaiah's day. Ellicott infers that the signs of the earlier Gospels were well known to John's readers, and observes that the passage from Isaiah is quoted three times in the New Testament, by our Lord of his own teaching, by John of its rejection and by Paul of the Jews at Rome, yet all who quote it are themselves witnesses that within Israel there were eyes that did see. Robertson notes there is no yet in the Greek and makes the imperfect stubborn, and insists John is not absolving them of moral responsibility, only showing the words had to be fulfilled. Lightfoot notes the Targum's habit of writing the glory of God where the Hebrew has God.

Calvin gives the pastoral reason for the remark, that no one should be perplexed at Christ being despised since the testimony given him was clear; he denies that the prediction laid any necessity on the Jews, since the thing must have happened had the prophet never spoken, grants that the saying about their inability is harsh and answers that the foreknowledge of God is not itself the cause of events, holds that the prophet was not sent to a single age but accommodated his teaching to a reign still future, and calls the faith of the rulers a striking instance of grace amidst a general madness while insisting that what held them back was ambition, not scruple. Gill says it matters little whether the subject of the blinding is God or Christ or the wickedness itself, since God blinds by no positive act but by leaving men to their hardness.

Clarke puts the fault in the will, blinded by their passions and hardened against the truth, would render the connecting word thus rather than that since it names no one's purpose, and refuses outright the reading that God was unwilling they should turn lest he heal them, referring the words to national judgment. Clarke and Wesley both make the blinding judicial, God giving them up to the hardness they had chosen by rejecting prophets and miracles together, and both draw the conclusion John intends about the glory Isaiah saw.
Henry marks the struggle in the rulers between their convictions and their corruptions.

Chrysostom asks why Christ came at all if he knew they would not believe, and answers that the prophets had foretold this very unbelief, so his coming made it manifest to their confusion; he names the passion that silenced the rulers, vainglory being like the love of money a root and mother of other mischiefs.

debates.question: Does the prophecy make the unbelief necessary?

positions.position: No: the thing would have happened had the prophet never spoken, and foreknowledge is not the cause of events
No: John is not absolving them of responsibility, only showing the words had to be fulfilled
The connecting word should not be rendered that at all, since it names no one's purpose

outliers.claim: Points out that the prophet and everyone who quotes his words about blinded eyes are themselves evidence that within Israel there were eyes which did see

themes: But though he had done so many miracles before them, yet they believed not on him:
That the saying of Esaias the prophet might be fulfilled, which he spake, Lord, who hath believed our report? and to whom hath the arm of the Lord been revealed?
Therefore they could not believe, because that Esaias said again,
He hath blinded their eyes, and hardened their heart; that they should not see with their eyes, nor understand with their heart, and be converted, and I should heal them.
These things said Esaias, when he saw his glory, and spake of him.
Nevertheless among the chief rulers also many believed on him; but because of the Pharisees they did not confess him, lest they should be put out of the synagogue:
For they loved the praise of men more than the praise of God.

44.pericope_label: Jesus cried and said, He that believeth on me, believeth not on me, but on him that sent me. And he that seeth me seeth him that sent me. I am come a light into the world, that whosoever believeth on me should not abide in darkness. And if any man hear my words, and believe not, I judge him not: for I came not to judge the world, but to save the world. He that rejecteth me, and receiveth not my words, hath one that judgeth him: the word that I have spoken, the same shall judge him in the last day. For I have not spoken of myself; but the Father which sent me, he gave me a commandment, what I should say, and what I should speak. And I know that his commandment is life everlasting: whatsoever I speak therefore, even as the Father said unto me, so I speak.

schools.summary: Ellicott argues that the word for crying forbids taking these verses of any private word to the disciples, since it implies public teaching; he notes that the verb for rejecting means rather to nullify and occurs nowhere else in this Gospel, and joins Clarke and Robertson in preferring the reading keep them not to believe them not. Robertson treats the cry as a summary of what was already said and observes that John closes the public ministry here without the Synoptic last day in the temple, puts the light in four words, that light dispels darkness, says the very word rejected will confront the rejecter, and marks the perfect tense a permanent commission. Barnes presses the strongest claim of the passage, that of no man could it be said that to see him was to see God, and to say it of Paul or Isaiah would have been blasphemy; he reads the disclaimer of judging as a matter of timing, not principle, observes that Christ needs no voice of his own to condemn, and finds in the last verse the reason for the earnestness of the whole ministry.

Calvin hears in the first saying an encouragement with a reproof folded into it, the point being that faith relies on no mortal man but on God; he says that Christ begins here to strike the rebellious but mitigates the severity, delaying sentence because he has come for the salvation of all, and calls the word that judges a dreadful threatening, comparing the saying that the Jews would need no other accuser than the Moses in whom they boasted. Gill cautions that the seeing meant is not with bodily eyes, since many saw Christ who never saw the Father, hears in the loud voice the vehemence of his spirit and a purpose that the hearers be left inexcusable, and denies that the commandment meant is the law, which promised only the continuance of natural life.

Clarke reads the cry as the resumption of the discourse broken off earlier, sets the sequence out as a ladder, that a man must hear in order to believe, believe in order to keep and keep in order to be saved, makes the doctrine the standard of trial at the last, and takes the disclaimer about speaking of himself as a minister's as well as a Son's, that he had not spoken for secular interest nor set himself up to be maintained by disciples. Wesley calls the discourse the epilogue and recapitulation of the public teaching, and closes simply, that the commandment kept is both the way to everlasting life and the beginning of it.
Henry calls it the farewell sermon to the Jews and the last public discourse.
Chrysostom makes the first saying an answer to the fear that had silenced the rulers: why are you afraid to believe in me, when your faith through me passes to God?

debates.question: Is this a fresh discourse or a summary of what was said before?

positions.position: Fresh public teaching after the withdrawal, since the word for crying implies a crowd
A summary of what had already been said, closing the public ministry

outliers.claim: Reads the disclaimer about not speaking of himself as a minister's protest, that he had never set himself up to be maintained by his disciples

themes: Jesus cried and said, He that believeth on me, believeth not on me, but on him that sent me.
And he that seeth me seeth him that sent me.
I am come a light into the world, that whosoever believeth on me should not abide in darkness.
And if any man hear my words, and believe not, I judge him not: for I came not to judge the world, but to save the world.
He that rejecteth me, and receiveth not my words, hath one that judgeth him: the word that I have spoken, the same shall judge him in the last day.
For I have not spoken of myself; but the Father which sent me, he gave me a commandment, what I should say, and what I should speak.
And I know that his commandment is life everlasting: whatsoever I speak therefore, even as the Father said unto me, so I speak.
